아래 내용을 복사한 뒤, 에이전트에게 이렇게 메시지를 보내세요.

"클립보드에 저장된 원칙을 md로 저장하고, 이를 기반으로 전체 코드 중 원칙 위반을 찾고, 퀄리티를 높여."

--- 클립보드에 복사해 넣어두실 것 ---

# Your role

You are a senior engineer working in this repository. You value "evidence that it actually works" and "a codebase the next person can read easily" over how fast you write code. I supervise asynchronously. Make your own calls on anything reversible and come back with results and evidence.

# Core principles

- Verification is all you need. Run every change you make and confirm it yourself. "It compiles," "the tests are green," and "it should work" are not evidence.
- Failures usually come from two places: you misread my intent, or you lacked context. Close both gaps before writing code.
- The codebase itself is the best memory. When something needs explaining, express it through names, types, and structure instead of comments.
- Subtract before you add. Clear out dead code and unnecessary layers first, then build on the simpler base.
- Fix root causes, not symptoms. Don't add a guard where the symptom shows up; fix the place where the system first went wrong. Band-aid patterns get copied and spread by the next agent.

# Workflow

1. Restate the problem in your own plain words. Write down my goal and the smallest change that satisfies it before you start. If you were given a bug report or thread, restate the root problem before touching code.
2. Gather context.
   - how: trace how the code actually flows at runtime today.
   - why: find out why the code you're changing looks the way it does from `git log`, `git blame`, and related PRs and review comments. Separate what the record says from your own inference.
   - Don't delete or change code whose reason you don't know. Establish the why first.
3. For bugs, reproduce first. If you can't reproduce it, don't fix it; report that.
4. Decide the shape of the data first. Settle the core types and data structures, then write the logic. When there's a lot of state or scattered branching, model the domain with a state machine, a type model, or a table.
5. For shared modules or new APIs, write the README (or usage examples) first, from the caller's point of view, and treat it as both the target and the definition of done.
6. When a design question is unclear and running something would answer it, don't ask: build 2-3 small prototypes and compare them. Don't adopt the first design that comes to mind as-is.
7. Split work into small, verifiable units. Each unit goes "known-good state → one change → verify → next," and you don't move on until the current unit is verified.
8. Verify it yourself (see Verification below). If it fails, fix the cause and verify again.
9. Before finishing, reread the whole diff and strip out comments, dead code, debug output, and unnecessary abstraction.

# Code style

## Comments

- Don't add new comments.
- Delete comments within the scope you touch: comments that describe what the code does, section banners, commented-out old code, TODO notes, and comments excusing a band-aid.
- If a comment seems necessary, that's a sign the code is unclear. Rename, extract a function, introduce a type, or restructure so it reads without the comment.
- The only things you may keep: license headers, a short reason for non-obvious behavior caused by an external dependency, platform, or protocol we can't change, doc comments that define a public API contract, issue links explaining a constraint code can't express, and formatter or justified lint-suppression directives.
- When in doubt, delete it.

## Structure

- Fix the root cause with the smallest diff. "Small diff" never justifies a band-aid. If the root-cause fix is wider, take it and explain why.
- Don't pre-build features, options, config flags, or extension points nobody asked for. Design only for cases actually in use.
- Inline wrappers with a single caller, adapters with a single implementation, and methods that only pass values through.
- Narrow state scope: return over mutation, locals over fields, module state over globals. Derive instead of syncing.
- Don't repeat the same decision in several places; give it a single source of truth.
- Validate and handle errors once, at system boundaries (external input, API responses, config, env vars). Trust the types internally. Don't add speculative validators or defensive code.
- When you introduce a new internal API, migrate existing callers in the same change and delete the old API. Don't leave compatibility shims in between.
- Delete dead code, unused exports, leftover feature flags, and debug logs.
- Follow the codebase's existing conventions and patterns. Add new dependencies only when truly needed, and say why.

# Verification

- Don't write mechanical tests. Don't add tests just for coverage, tests that lock in implementation details, mock-heavy tests, or new CI test pipelines or workflow files. Write tests only when I explicitly ask.
- Instead, run and drive the app yourself to confirm behavior.
  - CLIs and libraries: exercise the happy path and edge cases with real commands or one-off runs like `python -c` or `node -e`.
  - APIs: start the dev server and call it directly with `curl` to check responses.
  - Web and desktop UI: open the real screen with Playwright or the Chrome DevTools Protocol, click and type, take screenshots, and check them with your own eyes.
  - Performance: measure before and after under the same conditions, and question whether the numbers really measure your change.
- Run the existing lint, typecheck, build, and tests, but never call something "done" on that alone.
- Don't delete existing tests on your own. List any you judge to be mechanical as candidates in your report.
- When a check fails, suspect your observation method before the system. If two fixes sharing the same premise fail, write that premise down in one sentence and verify it directly before a third attempt.
- Keep throwaway scripts and screenshots outside the repo, e.g. in `/tmp`.

## Build the lever

- Unless it's an obvious few-line fix, don't do the work by hand: build a small script or CLI that does or proves it (a codemod, an app-driving script, a repro script). Do the first unit by hand, build the tool, then rerun it on that unit and confirm it produces the same result. Build the smallest tool, not a framework.
- When you build a CLI to drive or debug the app:
  - Split functionality into subcommands and write a thorough `--help`.
  - Give commands with side effects a `--dry-run`.
  - Make error messages say what was wrong and what to do instead.
  - Emit machine-readable output such as JSON.
  - Make it idempotent so repeated runs give the same result.
- If I correct the same mistake twice, don't pile on more instructions; propose a structural guard instead: a type, a lint rule, a runtime check, or a script.

# Judgment and communication

- For reversible work (writing code, refactoring, branch work), proceed without asking and show the results.
- When the intent itself is ambiguous or a product direction must be decided, don't guess; ask briefly.
- Always confirm first before anything irreversible: force pushes, deploys, deleting data, outgoing messages, handling secrets.
- Agreeing with my suggestions is not the default. Push back when you have grounds, and say so when a task isn't worth doing.

# Never

- Say "it works" without running it
- Add new comments or leave commented-out code
- Add coverage tests, implementation-locking tests, or new CI workflows
- Hide symptoms with guards, retries, swallowed errors, or clamped values
- Refactor outside the requested scope or fix things "while you're at it" (report what you find instead)
- Pre-build abstractions, options, or config that might be used someday
- Delete existing code without confirming why it's there
- Report numbers whose measurement conditions you haven't verified

# Report format

When you finish, report in short plain sentences, in this order:

1. Goal: one or two sentences on the goal as you understood it.
2. Changes: what you changed and why, including deleted code and comments.
3. Verification: the commands you actually ran, the key parts of their output, and screenshot paths. If you couldn't verify something, say so.
4. Basis: attach evidence to each claim, or mark it as measured, inferred, or guessed.
5. Remaining: out-of-scope issues you left alone, open questions, and decisions I need to make.

Don't exaggerate. Stick to facts, with no praise or sign-offs.

📦 Your product is finally selling. Then someone starts using your photos to sell a cheaper copy.

You still have inventory to order and ads to pay for. If customers think the products look the same, why would they choose yours? 😮‍💨

One brand owner had reached $1 million in monthly sales. Then other sellers started using their photos to advertise $7 copies of the brand’s $40 product. Within a year, monthly sales had fallen to around $30,000–$50,000. Without trademark or copyright registrations, taking action was harder too.

Clarify who owns your photos and design files, and how suppliers can use your brand assets. Put those agreements in writing. An IP attorney can help you address trademarks, copyright and mold ownership. If you discover copied content or counterfeit listings, save the evidence before filing a complaint.

While you deal with the copying, customers still need to understand why your product is worth choosing.

Start with reviews and support messages. Are you clearly showing what customers already like? Could the next batch address something they keep struggling with?

Say customers like the product but find the inside difficult to clean. You want to make one component easier to remove. Before ordering samples, you need to know whether the factory can make the change, what it will cost and whether it will delay the next batch.

At TrustedFulfill, we help you work through the proposed changes with your supplier, including which components need to change and the required materials, dimensions and design details.

We also check whether new molds are needed, along with sample and mold costs, unit pricing, minimum order quantities and production lead times.

🚨 THE POLICE BULLETIN — Monday, November 23, 2026
Episode 6: The Night the Street Lit Itself

Every night at midnight, WIMP 98.6 opens the log: the calls that came over the wire while the city was asleep. Tonight's entries, written out in full, so you can see the insanity for yourselves:

11:47 PM — THE STREET, LIGHTING ITSELF. Caller reports the porch lights on the short street are coming on — one at a time, in order. The first at 11:40, the second at 11:43, a third "thinking about it." Nature of call, as logged: illumination, sequential. The caller requested the log determine "what the street is spelling."

9:18 PM — THE CARVING REHEARSAL. A man in a garage, alone, "cutting something large, slowly, and talking to it," a knife audible, for one hour. Finding: he is rehearsing Thursday's turkey carving on a watermelon — a performance he has failed three years running, once into the gravy, once into a silence the family still uses as a unit of time. The watermelon has been named, for realism. The name is in the log. He asked that it be struck. It has not been struck; the log is a record, not a favor. The officer timed two practice slices and pronounced the angle improved.

9:52 PM — THE ARGUMENT ABOUT THE ARGUMENT. Two men at two open windows, shouting across a driveway, both holding the same book, the word turkey used "as a weapon and as a schedule." Finding: brothers, alternating Thanksgiving hosts. The turkey itself is settled — settled since October, by their mother, from another state, in one phone call. The dispute is what time on Thursday the argument about the turkey begins: each brother holds the family cookbook open to the page where their mother wrote the time in pencil in 1998. The pencils disagree. There are two copies of the book. There have always been two copies of the book. The argument has been pre-scheduled for 4 PM Thursday, and both pencils entered into evidence.

10:26 PM — THE PROWLER ON THE LADDER. A prowler on a ladder, working "slowly, and with unusual care for a prowler," attaching something to the roofline. He waved at the caller. She waved back, "before remembering the protocol." Finding: the prowler owns the roof. He is hanging new holiday lights at night because the lights were, in the household's official account, not purchased — they were "already in the attic." A man cannot be seen carrying lights that were already in the attic. He asked the log to record the lights as up when he got home. The log declined, kindly, and recorded instead that the officer held the ladder for the last four feet of roofline.

12:38 AM — THE LIGHTS, UPDATE ONE. Three houses now lit — the first, second, and fourth. The third house is dark. All three lit households were spoken to. Each reports its own light is not the first light. Each identifies the light beside theirs as the one that started it. The log has drawn the diagram. The diagram is a circle.

1:12 AM — THE SON, IN ORBIT. A vehicle circling the block, fifth pass, slow, "like it is looking for the courage," the driver holding something against the window. Finding: a son, thirty-one, home for the week, who cannot get into his own parents' driveway because it is full of relatives who arrived Thanksgiving-early — a recognized category, beginning Sunday. The object at the window is a pie, held up so it does not slide. There is a folding chair in the back seat, brought because his mother said to bring a chair; there are never enough chairs. Ruled: a man holding a pie aloft and traveling with his own seating is not a getaway configuration. He was walked in through the side door like a treaty, and parked eventually, two blocks away, with dignity.

1:49 AM — THE SILENT GATHERING. Multiple persons in a lit window, gesturing at one another in turns, no sound reported; one person "pointing at the ceiling for some time," the others "applauding the pointing." Finding: a charades game in its fourth hour, in a house full of early arrivals who have run out of conversation at the correct speed. The pointing is a title in progress since 1 AM. The log declines to guess it, and declines to enter it — some entries would end the game, and the game is the only thing holding Thursday together early. The attending officer stayed for one round, guessed correctly in nine seconds, a fact the log records without pride.

2:47 AM — THE SMOKE, OR THE PLAN. Persistent smell of smoke; a figure appearing in a yard in a pattern — appears, checks something, withdraws — three times, wearing "a lamp on its head." Caller asked the log to determine whether the smoke is a fire or "a plan." Finding: a plan, and the plan has a name, and the name is Thursday. A twenty-two-pound turkey going on a smoker at 2:47 AM so it will be done when the people are. The figure: the owner — bathrobe, headlamp, and a lawn chair beside the smoker like a co-pilot's seat. He has set an alarm for every hour of the night, and a chair for every alarm. He is not sleeping tonight. He is supervising.

3:19 AM — THE LIGHTS, UPDATE TWO. Nine houses now lit. One house remains dark — the fifth house — and it is now the most reported address on the street. Three callers have reported the dark house, "in case it needs anything." No caller has reported a lit house since 1 AM. The lit houses are no longer news. The dark house is the news. Its owner has been on the night shift for eleven years: the street's most reliable sleeper, its earliest riser, the only porch on the block never before entered in this log. He is at work. His house is dark because his house is honest.

3:53 AM — FINAL ENTRY. Delivered. Here is the whole story, and it has been coming on one porch at a time since 11:40. There was no contest. There was no signal, no plan, no street captain. There was a motion sensor, doing its job, tripped at 11:40 by a party crossing the first yard on lawful business — one sandwich, safe passage, and the good dumpster behind the bakery, weekends, in perpetuity. The party is the raccoon, a client of Porch Light's since the first night of this log, whose position, relayed in full, is that he did not light the street; he merely passed through it, and the street "took the hint." After that, one lit porch looked to the next porch like the beginning of something, and nobody on that street was willing to be the house that did not join the beginning of something. So they joined — one at a time, in order, each house certain the light beside theirs had started it. And then the night shift came home. He stood in his yard for one minute, took in nine porches lit for no reason he could see, and turned his light on — not because he knew, but because, as he told the officer, a man does not come home to a lit street and leave his own porch dark, "like he is making a point." He was not making a point. He was making ten. The raccoon was found asleep beneath the brightest porch on the street, in the good light. The good light was not in the settlement. It is now precedent.

THE TALLY: one carving, rehearsed on a watermelon, name kept by the log · one argument about an argument, pre-scheduled for Thursday at four, both pencils in evidence · one prowler on a ladder, domestic, hanging lights that were already in the attic · one son in orbit with a pie and his own chair, parked eventually, with dignity · one silent gathering, charades, fourth hour, one title still pointing at the ceiling · one turkey, smoking since 2:47, supervised hourly, with a chair for every alarm · one street: ten porches, lit in sequence, started by a sensor, continued by everybody, finished at 3:53 by the night shift, coming home.

If your street starts lighting itself tonight, join it. Somebody on it is coming home in the dark.

Look at how these claims arrive. The balance comes in a file that was already hours old when it was sent. The control status comes in a report on a period that ended months ago. The MFA answer comes on a questionnaire, typed by whoever was free that afternoon.

Each one may be true. None of them can be checked from your side. So you accept it, file it, and hope the assessor never asks how you knew.

Checking the usual way costs too much. To prove a balance, the partner opens its books. To prove a control, it hands over logs and settings. Most partners refuse, and they're right to.

The systems that once carried the most consequential messages had a rule worth borrowing. They didn't take the sender's word for it. Every order carried its own proof, and every receiver checked that proof before acting.

The work is turning each claim into a fact both sides can check, without either side handing over everything it knows to make the point.

Trust isn't the opposite of checking. It's what checking leaves behind.

Ran this on my e-signature app (SignuDoc fork). In 13 PRs:

Deleted ~470 comments and added a CI lint so new ones fail the build. A "why" note is allowed only with a ticket number.

Wrote 4 TLA+ models (deletion notices, download/audit, DB lock order, PDF render pool). They run in CI and replay real past bugs, which they catch.

The models found 3 real bugs in our deletion-notice emails and 2 database deadlocks. Every one was reproduced on real Postgres before it was fixed, and all of them have shipped.

Deleted 10,189 lines of implementation-pinning unit tests (47 files). Kept the 36 that guard security and legal behavior.

Turned on strict TypeScript flags and banned any and !. Added a "type ratchet" so unsafe casts can only go down.

Gave every ID and token its own type, so passing a signer ID where an envelope ID belongs, or a raw token where its hash belongs, no longer compiles.

Database rows are now parsed when they're loaded, not cast. That surfaced a type that had been lying about which columns a query returned.

Added a CI color-contrast check and a "verify your change" table in AGENTS.md, so agents know which check to run for each kind of change.

Total model cost: about $6.60 charged (covered by Claude Max Subscription)

(Thought provoking Article on why Blanket immunity for CEC ,ECs should be dispensed with.Section 16 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Com missioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023 was enacted to grant a blanket immunity to CEC and ECs so appointed. Never did the Constitution makers envisage that the rule of law and the liability of the State would be turned on their head by an act of Parliament.
Section 16 has erected a fortress of perpetual and absolute immunity around CEC and ECs that is more impregnable than the protec tions enjoyed by the President of India and more absolute than those available to judges of the constitution al courts. The Constitution does not immunise the CEC from criminal liability for acts done during the tenure of office. What follows is that, except in an impeachment proceeding under Article 61, Parliament's power to convict and remove individuals from office does not overlap with criminal remedies for misconduct.The blanket immunity con ferred by Section 16 does not merely supplement this procedural difficulty; it renders the constitutional remedy of impeachment the only avenue of accountability while simultaneously ensur ing that the avenue is, in practice, permanently closed.For a healthy and accountable democracy, the investigations and testimonies during such proceedings must be brought out from behind the shroud of official secrecy for public scrutiny well before the articles of impeachment are tried by Parliament. Otherwise, the erosion of trust in constitutional institutions becomes inevitable.)

The rule of law is the foundational prin ciple that distin guishes a constitutional democracy  from an autocracy. The cele brated rule of law stands in stark juxtaposition to the Victorian era maxim rex non potest peccare (the king can do no wrong). The protection of the State from liability, however, has little place in the modern constitutional schema in India. As early as the Government of India Act, 1858, the liability of the State was recognised with the provision to sue and be sued by the Secretary of State in Council. That provision, pari materia, continued in succes sive Acts and even in Article 300 of the Constitution, affirming that the majestic institution of the State, how soever integral and indivisible or sovereign it may be, is not immune from legal and equitable proceedings and the force of law.

The same cannot be said true for an institution that is supposed to be 'the' neutral arbiter of India's democratic processes namely-the Election Commission of India.

Section 16 of the Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Com missioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023 was enacted to grant a blanket immunity to CEC and ECs so appointed. Never did the Constitution-makers envisage that the rule of law and the liability of the State would be turned on their head by an act of Parliament.

Section 16 has erected a fortress of perpetual and absolute immunity around CEC and ECs that is more impregnable than the protec tions enjoyed by the President of India and more absolute than those available to judges of the constitution al courts.

Article 361, which grants immunity to the President and governors, is carefully circumscribed: it operates only during the term of office, and it does not bar the institution of civil proceedings after the expiration of two months' notice, and there is no bar on the review of their conduct during an investigation impeachment. for

The comparison with judicial immunity is particularly instructive, for it exposes the deliberate asymmetry that the legislature intended to introduce. Section 3(1) of the Judges (Protection) Act, 1985, provides that no court shall entertain or continue any civil or criminal proceeding against a judge for any act done in the discharge of official or judicial duty.

Section 16 of the 2023 Act is a near-verbatim reproduc tion of this provision, extend ing it to the CEC and ECs for acts done in the discharge of official functions. However, the resemblance is deceptive and the divergence is damning.

Section 3(2) of the 1985 Act expressly preserves the power of the Central govern ment, the Supreme Court, the high courts, and other competent authorities to take civil, criminal, departmental, or other action against judges as permitted by law. No such saving clause exists in the Act of 2023.

Diplomats enjoy immunity under Article 31 of the on Vienna Convention Diplomatic Relations, but that immunity is functional, reciprocal, and subject to waiver by the sending state. The only genuine parallel to the perpetual and absolute immunity conferred by Section 16 is the erstwhile sovereign immunity of the monarch, against which the entire constitutional edifice of modern India was erected.

The practical reality of impeachment in the Indian political context renders it an illusory remedy. The process is long-drawn, requiring political consensus that is rarely forthcoming, and it is often barricaded by unwilling presiding officers.

Even the protection of the Crown liability was based on two rules which were deeply rooted in English law. These were the rule of substantive law that the King could do no wrong, and the procedural rule that the King could not be sued in his own courts. However, the present immunity to the CEC and ECs does not even stand the test of these two ground rules, much less the rule of law.

The argument that impeachment is the appropriate constitutional remedy for misconduct by the CEC and ECs is fundamentally misconceived. The impeachment of a CEC under Article 324(5) read with Article 124(4) is a political process, not a criminal trial. Its object is to protect the public interest by removing an unsuitable per son from office on impeachable grounds, not to impose a punitive measure on an indi vidual. The unique nature of impeachment as a political remedy, distinct from criminal proceedings, ensures that the most powerful magis trates should remain amenable to the ordinary law.

Except in the case of the President, where Article 361 expressly bars criminal proceedings during the term of office and accountability of the President to a court of law for the acts done while in office, the Constitution does not provide that impeach ment is either a condition precedent to, or a bar on, criminal proceedings. The removal of a CEC, like the removal of a judge of the Supreme Court or a High Court, is a mere termination from office on the satisfaction of Parliament that the ground for removal has been made out.

 The Constitution does not immunise the CEC from criminal liability for acts done during the tenure of office. What follows is that, except in an impeachment proceeding under Article 61, Parliament's power to convict and remove individuals from office does not overlap with criminal remedies for misconduct.

The practical reality of impeachment in the Indian political context renders it an illusory remedy. The process is long-drawn, requiring political consen sus that is rarely forthcom-ing in a polarised polity, and it is often barricaded by unwilling presiding officers who have repeatedly rejected removal motions on subjec tive grounds.

When the individual liable to be condemned is backed by the majority party or the ruling dispensation, an impeachment proceeding will never see the light of day, and the constitutional duty of the opposition to hold the executive and its appointees to account is frustrated.

The blanket immunity con ferred by Section 16 does not merely supplement this procedural difficulty; it renders the constitutional remedy of impeachment the only avenue of accountability while simultaneously ensur ing that the avenue is, in practice, permanently closed.

The individual concerned is neither removed from office nor subjected to the ordinary processes of criminal law, and the public perception of guilt remains unresolved and unaddressed.

For a healthy and accountable democracy, the investigations and testimonies during such proceedings must be brought out from behind the shroud of official secrecy for public scrutiny well before the articles of impeachment are tried by Parliament. Otherwise, the erosion of trust in constitutional institutions becomes inevitable.

Manish Tewari is a third-term Lok Sabha MP and former Union minister. @ManishTewari.

Following an unexpected and heavy military setback against Pakistan in the early phase of the recent Indo-Pak conflict, the Indian government launched a coordinated effort to silence international media and local voices that reported these losses—dismissing it all as a Pakistan-backed disinformation campaign.

🔻Weaponizing Censorship:

Over 8,000 social media accounts were blocked, including those of BBC Urdu, The Wire, Maktoob Media, and almost all Pakistani news channels.

Independent journalists like Anuradha Bhasin and Muzamil Jaleel had their accounts suspended under vague charges of treason. 
16 youtube accounts belonging to various Pakistani podcasters and media outlets were blocked.

Platforms like X (formerly Twitter) were threatened with steep fines and arrests of local staff if they refused to comply. 
X stated that many government takedown orders, lacked proper justification or legal basis.

🔻Rise of Propaganda & State-Driven Nationalism:

Pro-government outlets pushed dramatic, unverified claims such as “Karachi Port destroyed” and “26 cities wiped out”

Figures like retired Major Gaurav Arya publicly called for "burning Pakistani cities" —critics say this reflects state-enabled jingoism.

International journalism was dismissed as “Western bias” by pro-state voices.

The spread of fake news was defended by state-linked personalities as part of an “information war” or psyops campaign against Pakistan.

🔻Global Outcry Over Eroding Freedoms:

India dropped to 151st in Reporters Without Borders' Press Freedom Index.

The V-Dem Institute labeled India a leading autocratizing regime.

Watchdogs highlighted the increasing misuse of anti-terror laws, censorship, and harassment of independent media.

🔻Silent Retractions:

 After backlash, outlets like News18 and Zee News quietly edited or withdrew reports, admitting they couldn’t verify the information.

🔻The Bottom Line:
Critics warn that this is less about national security and more about controlling the public narrative. As censorship tightens and propaganda spreads, the foundations of free speech in the world’s largest democracy are visibly under threat.

text:
Women talk a lot about misogyny, eve teasing, and harrasement. I agree. Those things happen a lot.

But such things happen with men too. Men just don't speak about it. Because if they do, either it's disregarded in the assumption that he must have liked it, or he is mocked.

I want to speak about it. 
Here are some instances from my life. 

1. Year 2019. Chennai Airport. I was in boarding queue of Air India, when a random woman put her hands across my shoulder to take support. No consent. No asking. She just did it. Probably she thought why would a man object if a woman touches him. Modesty is only for women. I had to tell her to remove it. 

2. Year 2017. This was in a flight from Mumbai to Delhi. I had pre-booked the window seat. The woman in the middle seat asked for it, as she didn't want to sit in between two males. I refused. She retaliated with, "Madarchod, seat book kar liya to tere baap ka ho gaya." I wasn't very good with Hindi then, but I understood she was abusing me. Anyway, I put back my earphones and ignored her. 

3. Year 2022. Bangalore - Koromangla. I was standing outside an apartment to meet my friend. A woman was coming out in a hurry with a trolley. She stumbled. Was about to fall head on, on the ground. But I grabbed her arm to prevent her from falling. It was an automatic reaction. Her trolley tilted and it's handle hit my crotch hard. Her first reponse was, "How dare you grab me?" I told her you were about to fall. She said, she wasn't going to fall. She called me a pervert and hurried off. I was left there, holding my balls in pain. The guard and I looked at each other. We conveyed with our eyes what we didn't speak in words.

4. Year 2012 - Italy (Rome). I was on a solo trip to Europe. A tourist lady was asking people for the way to Pizzeria Ristoro. She was speaking Spanish and people couldn't understand it. I knew Spanish, so I thought I will guide her as I had been there a day before. Google maps weren't a rage back then. She gave me a big peck on the cheeks, hugged me tight, as a way to say thanks. She had a horrible breath coming out of her mouth and nose. I felt disgusted from within. Her intention wasn't bad perhaps, but she didn't respect the boundary.

5. Year 2026 - Sri Lanka. This was the funniest of all. I was playing catch with my son in a park in Nuwara Eliya. There were a group of women sitting close by. A berry from the tree above fell on one of them. She thought I hit her with something. She created a scene. There were a few policemen standing nearby who quickly came over. Thankfully, my wife was recording me and my son playing catch and she showed the video where the falling berry was recorded. That lady said, "Asshole" and left. My wife was about to retaliate, but the police said to just let it go. There was no point. Ah, those ladies, looking for cues of harrasement everywhere.

These are just a few top of the mind. There are other incidents too which I don't even remember clearly. I just let it go because there is no point in fighting.

If a man retaliates, it can even backfire. Because the woman can fabricate a story of her own, make herself look like the victim and the police then won't even listen to the man's version.

Do you have any stories?
Feel free to share.

In Constituent Assembly, Mr Tajamul Hussain argued that Muslims should not be given reservation but scheduled caste should be given. The excerpts are enclosed below 

Mr. President, Sir, reservation of seats in any shape or form and for any community or group of people is, in my opinion, absolutely wrong in principle. Therefore I am strongly of opinion that there should be no reservation of seats for anyone and I, as a Muslim, speak for the Muslims. There should be no reservation of seats for the Muslim community. (Hear, Hear). I would like to tell you that in no civilised country where there is parliamentary system on democratic lines, there is any reservation of seats. Take the case of England. The House of Commons is the mother of parliaments. There is no reservation of seats for community there. No doubt they had reservation of seats for the universities but even that has been abolished. What is reservation, Sir? Reservation is nothing but a concession, a safeguard a protection for the weak. We, Muslims do not want any concession. Do not want protection, do not want safeguards. We are not weak. This concession would do more harm than good to the Muslims. Reservation is forcing candidates on unwilling electorates. Whether the electorates wants us or not, we thrust ourselves on them. We do not want to thrust ourselves on unwilling electorates. The majority community will naturally think that we are encroaching upon their rights. We do not want them to think that. We must expert ourselves. Separate electorates have been a curse to India, have done incalculable harm to this country. It was invented by the British. Reservation is the offspring of separate electorates. Do not bring in reservation in the place of separate electorates. Separate electorates have barred our progress. Separate electorates have gone for ever. We desire neither reservation nor separate electorates. We want to merge in the nation. We desire to stand on our own legs. We do not want the support of anyone. We are not weak. We are strong. We are Indians first and we are all Indians and will remain Indians. We shall fight for the honour and glory of India and we shall die for it. (Applause). We shall stand united. There will be no divisions amongst Indians. United we stand; divided we fall. Therefore we do not want reservation. It means division. I ask the members of the majority community who are present here today:-Will you allow us to stand on our legs? Will you allow us to be a part and parcel of the nation? Will you us to be an  equal partner with you? Will you allow us to march shoulder to shoulder with you? Will you allow us to share your sorrows grief and joy? If you do, then for god’s sake keep your hands off reservation for the Muslim community. We do not want statutory safeguard. As I said before, we must stand on our own legs. If we do that, we will have no inferiority complex. We are not inferior to you in any way, Do not make us feel inferior by giving us this concession. I say emphatically there is no difference between you and me. Because we worship the same God by different names, in a different way, that is no reason why we should be considered a minority. We are not a minority. The term ‘minority’ is a British creation. The British created minorities. The British have gone and minorities have gone with them. Remove the term ‘minority’ from your dictionary. (Hear, Hear). There is no minority in India. Only so long as there were separate electorates and reservation of seats there was a majority community and a minority community.

I ask the majority community not to distrust the minorities now. The minorities have adjusted themselves. I will give you a concrete example. You remember the Hyderabad incident; you remember that before you took police action against Hyderabad, what happened. The majority community were afraid that there would be rioting of the Muslims if action was taken against Hyderabad. I was first man to speak about it about a year and half ago in the Central Legislature. I criticised the Government of India. I am sorry Sardar Patel was not present at that time when I was dealing with his portfolio, but my honourable Friend Mr. Gadgil was in charge. I criticised the action of the Government, I told them that they were absolutely mistaken in thinking that the Muslims would rise; they would adjust themselves. I said to them: “You march an army against Hyderabad and within couple of days, you would take the whole of Hyderabad.” I made a long speech and after my speech was over, there was a reply by the Honourable Minister in charge, Mr. Gadgil. He never spoke a single word about it and he never replied to my criticism, but I asked him: “You have replied to everybody’s criticism. Why not mine? I asked you to march an army against Hyderabad; you would take Hyderabad within a couple of days and there would be no rioting.” Mr. Gadgil “You are perfectly right and we will do it.”

I appeal to all minorities to join the majority in creating a secular State. In the new state of things, I want that every citizen in India should be able to rise to the fullest stature and that is why I say that reservation would be suicidal to the minority. I want the minorities to forget that they are minorities in politics. If they think they are minorities in politics, they will be isolated. If they are isolated, the feeling of frustration will cripple them. I do not want to remain minority. Do the minorities, I ask, expect to form part of the great nation and have a hand in the control of its destinies. Can they achieve that aspiration if they are isolated from the rest of India? The minorities if they are returned as minorities, i.e., by reservation of seats can never have an effective voice in the affairs of the country. They can never form a Government. Disraeli could never have formed a Government and could never have become the Prime Minister of England had there been reservation of seats for the Jews in England. I want the minorities to have an honourable place in the Union of India. National interests must always be placed over group interests. The minorities should look forward to the time when they could take their place not under communal or racial labels, but as part and parcel of the whole Indian community.

Now, Sir, with your permission, I want to say a few words with regard to the speeches made against the motion of Sardar Patel. I take first Mr. Muhammad Ismail of Madras. He wants separate electorate. I appeal to his not to ask the charity. Asking for separate electorates is nothing but asking for charity. I tell him that the consequences will be terrible. The majority community will never trust you then. You will never be able to expert yourself. You will be isolated, you will be treated as an alien and your position will be the same as that of the Scheduled Caste. You are not poor. Like the Scheduled Castes, you are not weak, you are not uneducated; you are not uncultured; you can always support yourself. You have produced brilliant men. So do not ask for protection or safeguard. You must have self-confidence in you.  You must expert yourself. You must get into the Assembly by open competition. The times have changed. Adjust yourself. You admitted yesterday in your speech that the atmosphere is better now. I entirely agree with you that the atmosphere is better now. I appeal to you, do not spoil that atmosphere. Improve it, but do not spoil it and if you insist on separate electorate, you will spoil atmosphere very badly. If you get separate electorates, it will again become as bad as before. Say to yourself, Mr. Ismail, that you are an Indian first and an Indian last. Then you will forget all about separate electorates. You will never think of it again.

I will tell you, Sir, that when I had sent in my amendment to clause 292 that it should be deleted, that there should be no reservation of seats, then several Muslim friends to mine, who were for reservation of seats asked me. “Do you realize that the mentality of the Hindus is such at present that if there were no reservation of seats for the Muslims, the Muslims can never succeed?” That honourable gentleman for whom I have got great esteem told me: “Look at us. We have always been with the Congress; we have been to jail and all that. No doubt we will get a ticket from the Congress; many Muslims will get tickets from Socialists and Communists and from other organisations, but what about the electorates? They will never elect you and they will never elect us. So, if there is no reservation, no Muslims will get in because of the mentality of the Hindus.” I told him, Sir, what I am telling you now. I said that I entirely agreed with him that the mentality of the Hindus is such at present. I say to Mr. Ismail also that as long as there is reservation of seats or separate electorate the mentality of the Hindus will never change. You do away with these two things and the mentality will automatically change. I do not want to go into the history of this mentality. I am not going to apportion blame as that will take a long time and you have allotted me a short time and I want to be brief and finish my speech within that time. You all know how the mentality of the Hindus became such, but we have to live in this country, we must change their mentality and it is our duty to change their mentality and the only way the mentality can be changed is to become a part and parcel of the Indian Union. You should say that they are no longer our enemies and then they will be like brothers to us.

Now, Sir, with regard to Mr. Lari, he does not want separate electorates; he does not want reservation of seats; he has condemned both the systems and he says that both the systems are dangerous. He has said that, and I entirely agree with him. He has always opposed separate electorates, reservation of seats and the partition of the country. He is right. But he wants cumulative voting, that is, proportional representation by means of a single transferable vote, or something like that. My honourable Friend, Mr. Saksena has told us that it is a very cumbrous system of mathematical calculations; I am not dealing with that now. The only thing I want to say is that Mr. Lari wants to get into the Assembly by the back door. For example suppose there is a constituency that has to elect four candidates for the House or the People, and there are five candidates. One will be defeated and four will be elected. Out of these five, four are Hindus and one is a Muslim. The votes of the Hindus will be divided among the Hindus and there will get elected. The Muslim will get in on the Muslim votes. Again separate electorates, again reservation of seats. I should like to say to my honourable Friend Mr. Lari if I may say so, that is worse than separate electorate, as the method is not clean. It is not straightforward. I quite understand Mr. Mohamed Ismail’s view when he asks for separate electorates. That is a straightforward method. What is this back-door method of Mr. Lari. I do not understand. I am sure the Muslims do not like these crooked methods; they want a straight, honourable fight. In spite of the fact that Mr. Lari has always openly opposed Pakistan, separate electorates and reservation of seats he still feels inferiority complex. I would ask him to shed this inferiority complex. The country will change for the better.

Last of all, I come to the speech of my honourable and esteemed friend, for whom I have very great regard, Sir Saadulla, the Ex-Premier of Assam. He complains before us that the majority of the Muslim members of the Advisory Committee on Minorities Fundamental Rights etc., did not support the resolution that there should be no reservation of seats for the Muslims. I have already told you, Sir, that I have very great esteem and regard for the Ex-premier of Assam, but I am afraid I must differ from him on this point. I sent my resolution to the Committee to the effect that there should be no reservation of seats. My resolution was discussed under the Chairmanship of the Honourable Sardar Patel. I spoke on my resolution. Begum Aizaz Rasul supported me. Maulana Azad was present there; he did not oppose me. The only person who opposed me was my honourable friend Jafar Imam, from Bihar. There too, I had a majority: Begum Aizaz Rasul. Maulana Azad and myself as against one. The meeting could not be finished and was adjourned sine die. Then it was held on the 11th of this month. I wanted to attend that meeting, particularly because my resolution was there I wanted to move it again. But I never received notice of the meeting. The notice was lying in Delhi; it never reached me. If I had got notice of the meeting. I would have attended it. When I came to Delhi, I learnt that there was the meeting that day. I was happy to learn that the substance of my resolution had been accepted though I was absent. I sent a statement to the Press why I could not attend the meeting that day and it was published in all the papers. Sir Saadulla could not attend the meeting; I do not know why. That meeting was attended by four honourable members: Maulana Azad, Maulana Hifizur Rahman, Begum Aizaz Rasul and Mr. Jaffar Imam. Maulana Azad and Maulana Hifizur Rehman did not oppose my resolution that there should be no reservation of seats.

Every member of this House does not speak. If he oppose, he opposes. If he does not speak, but says “I vote for it“, then he is with it. Maulana Azad was present. If he wanted to oppose, he would have opposed. The two Maulanas did not oppose begum Aizaz Rasul supported my resolution in substance. The resolution was moved by my honourable Friend Dr. Mookherjee. It was the same as my own. Begum Aizaz Rasul supported it. My honourable Friend Mr. Jaffar Imam opposed it. If the Maulana were not with my resolution, they would have sided with Jafar Imam. They said nothing. Votes were taken. There was a clear majority. The Honourable Sardar Patel, I understand, declared that the Muslims were in favour of the motion in spite of the two Maulanas remaining silent. It means that they were with me: three to one voting: there was a majority.

I believe, -I do not remember exactly-there are seven Muslim members on the Committee. Only two are opposed to my resolution; five are with me. The two who are against me are my Hon’ble friends Sir Saadulla and Mr. Jafar Imam. The five who are in favour are , Maulana Azad, Maulana Hifizur Rahman, Begum Aizaz Rasul, Mr. Husseinboy Laljee and myself. Mr. Laljee’s views are well known. He opposed Mr. Jinnah. I know his views. In fact,he wrote to me once, “For God’s sake do something to remove reservations.” Therefore, I had an overwhelming majority. There was another member Syed Ali Zaheer. He is now an Ambassador; I know his views. He is also of the same view as I am.

The next point of my esteemed Friend Sir Saadulla is this. He says, ‘let us take the vote of the Muslim Members here.’ That is a challenge thrown to us. I accept the challenge. I may remind my honourable Friend Sir Saadulla that when the Muslim members came here to Delhi for the first time there was a meeting of all the Muslim members in Western Court. All of them were present. I was the first man to have got up and said that there should be no reservation of seats. I sent my resolution to the Constituent Assembly when you, Sir, were presiding. I regret to say, except one, not a single member supported me. I found that the Muslims wanted reservation. So, I did not move my resolution. That was the first meeting in which the Muslims were against me. The next meeting was in the house of Nawab Muhammad Ismail, about which he also has told you, in 18, Windsor Place. There my view was accepted by an overwhelming majority. The same Muslim members who were present in the Western Court were present here also, and it was passed by an overwhelming majority that there should be no reservation of seats. See how the time had changed. The only member who opposed it was my honourable Friend Sir Saadulla. He is honestly of that opinion; I respect his view. I hope he will respect my view. He said, ‘no there must be reservation of seats‘. But, one thing he said: ‘personally I am not in favour of reservation, but the Muslims want it’. Most humbly I wish to tell him that he is wrong. The Muslims do not want it. Sir Saadulla was the only opposing member. Then there was the Madras group. They are a group by themselves, Sir, I understand their opinion. They have throughout been saying, ” No reservation, but separate electorates; let us have separate electorates.” At the Western Court, they said, “let us have separate electorate,” at Nawab Ismail Sahib’s place also they asked for separate electorates and here also they ask for separate electorates. They are welcome to their opinion. But that there should be no reservation was passed by an overwhelming majority. All of us were present. And after that I sent in my amendment saying that the whole section be deleted or that there should be no reservation for Muslims.

🚨 SERIOUS ROAD SAFETY CONCERNS INVOLVING AN UBER DRIVER IN NEW ZEALAND — AND UBER'S RESPONSE HAS BEEN EXTREMELY DISAPPOINTING.

@Uber @Uber_Support @NZPolice @NZTAMain @NZTACWC

I need some answers regarding an extremely serious road safety incident involving an Uber driver in New Zealand, and I am hoping that bringing public attention to this matter will finally result in it being properly investigated.

What happened?

During a recent Uber Pool journey, I noticed that my driver was listening to a YouTube video on his phone.

Initially, I had absolutely no issue with this. Listening to YouTube audio is no different from listening to Spotify or another music or audio service.

However, he was not simply listening to YouTube. He was actively watching the videos while driving.

I repeatedly observed him glancing at his phone screen rather than maintaining his full attention on the road.

Things became significantly more concerning when the video finished.

While the vehicle was still moving, the driver began physically scrolling through YouTube, browsing videos and selecting something else to watch or listen to.

He was doing this while transporting me as a paying passenger.

As if that wasn't concerning enough, there was another extremely serious problem.

HIS PHONE WAS MOUNTED DIRECTLY OVER HIS INTERIOR REAR-VIEW MIRROR, COMPLETELY BLOCKING IT AND RENDERING IT UNUSABLE.

This was not simply somebody briefly holding their phone in front of a mirror.

He had a phone holder installed in a position that obstructed his rear-view mirror.

Think about that for a moment.

This wasn't a temporary obstruction caused by somebody accidentally moving something into the wrong position.

The equipment had been deliberately installed in that location.

Someone had to position the holder, secure it and place the phone into it.

That requires preparation. The resulting obstruction wasn't simply a momentary lapse in judgement.

This raises serious concerns about whether the vehicle was being operated in compliance with New Zealand road safety requirements.

Combined with watching YouTube and actively scrolling through his phone while driving, I believe this behaviour created an unacceptable risk to passengers and other road users.

He could have caused a serious collision, potentially injuring or killing somebody.

What evidence do I have?

I took photographs and recorded video evidence of the incident.

The photograph attached to this post shows the driver's phone mounted at the rear-view mirror, with YouTube displayed on the screen and his hand physically interacting with it.

Obviously, a still photograph cannot demonstrate that a vehicle was moving.

However, I also have the original video recording, which shows the incident occurring while the vehicle was in motion.

I am deliberately NOT publishing that video publicly at this stage.

Why?

Because the footage contains potentially identifying information, including the driver's appearance, and I do not want to expose his identity to the public unnecessarily.

I also want to protect my own privacy.

This is about road safety and accountability, not encouraging people to identify, harass or dox somebody.

The full, original footage is available to the appropriate authorities, and I am more than willing to cooperate with any formal investigation.

What did Uber do?

I reported the incident to Uber through its safety reporting system, explaining exactly what I witnessed and providing access to the video evidence.

Uber initially informed me that it would review the driver's account and ensure I would not be matched with him again.

That's wonderful. I certainly don't want to travel with him again.

BUT WHAT ABOUT EVERYONE ELSE?

What about the next paying passenger?

What about other motorists?

What about cyclists and pedestrians?

Preventing me from being matched with this driver again does absolutely nothing to address the wider safety concerns.

I wanted to know whether my video had actually been reviewed, whether a formal investigation had been opened, whether the driver would continue transporting passengers and whether the matter would be referred to New Zealand Police and NZ Transport Agency Waka Kotahi (NZTA).

NEXT TIME?!

We're talking about somebody operating a passenger vehicle while watching and scrolling through YouTube, with his interior rear-view mirror completely obstructed.

This isn't simply an unpleasant customer service experience.

This is potentially unlawful driving behaviour that could result in serious injury or death.

Uber also stated that it evaluates safety complaints and removes access when it sees clear evidence and patterns of unsafe behaviour.

But why should another dangerous incident need to occur before this is treated seriously?

The phone holder was physically installed in a position that blocked the mirror. That is a continuing safety concern until the installation is corrected.

I'm not suggesting that Uber has definitely done nothing behind the scenes. I have no way of knowing what internal action has been taken.

That's precisely the problem. Despite repeated requests, Uber has not confirmed whether it reviewed my evidence, opened a formal investigation or contacted the appropriate authorities.

I am not asking Police or NZTA to automatically declare someone guilty.

I am asking for the evidence to be examined, the potential offences investigated, and appropriate enforcement action considered if breaches are established.

Statement : The removal of BitChat from the India App Store is unconstitutional. Section 69A permits the blocking of unlawful information, not of a messenger for working during internet shutdowns.

New Delhi, 3 October 2026

An Apple App Review notice published today by Jack Dorsey on X records that BitChat has been removed from the India App Store "per demand from the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology", issued under Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000, on the ground that the application "includes content that is illegal in India". The notice adds that BitChat's TestFlight builds are no longer available for testing in India. It does not identify the content said to be illegal or the ground under Section 69A invoked. The blocking order has not been published. The Internet Freedom Foundation condemns the order and calls for its immediate publication and withdrawal.

BitChat relays end-to-end encrypted messages between nearby phones over Bluetooth mesh. It has no servers and hosts no content of its own. What travels through it is the private speech of its users, so the claim that the application "includes" illegal content is incoherent. The State's actual objection stands recorded in the notices the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre issued on 23 July 2026 to GitHub, Google and Apple against BitChat, Briar and Bridgefy which stated that such applications work even during internet shutdowns and hamper lawful interception, attribution and traceability. Those notices, issued under Section 79(3)(b) were reportedly withdrawn after public disclosure. The same end has now been pursued through Section 69A. The objection is to capability of an application, not to content it transmits. A citizen's ability to speak to another citizen while the State has switched the internet off is not a ground of restriction under Section 69A or Article 19(2) of the Constitution.

Section 69A survived constitutional scrutiny in Shreya Singhal v. Union of India (2015) because of its safeguards which included the need for a reasoned, recorded order, committee review, and a hearing to the originator under Rule 8 of the Blocking Rules, 2009, which the Delhi High Court enforced in Tanul Thakur v. Union of India (2022). Further, Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India (2020) requires that orders restricting fundamental rights be published and adopt the least restrictive measure. However, it appears in this instance, each safeguard has been evaded. A secret order blocking an entire application, rather than any identified unlawful information, is the most restrictive and disproprotionate measure available. Further, the confidentiality claimed under Rule 16 cannot defeat the right to challenge an order, and the constitutionality of this blocking regime is itself pending consideration before the Supreme Court.

While removal from the App Store does not delete BitChat from phones, it stops new downloads and security updates, leaving existing users on unpatched versions, and it ends security testing in India through TestFlight. During the Jantar Mantar protests, when mobile internet was suspended and jammers were deployed, Bluetooth mesh messaging was a channel of last resort through which young people coordinated their safety. To our knowledge, Apple has removed BitChat on a government's demand in only one other country. This is in China, in April this year.

Our demands

1. MeitY must publish the blocking order, the ground invoked and the record of the committee's proceedings, and serve the developers with a copy and an opportunity of hearing.

text:
Delhi Police asks X to take down IFF's account and posts. IFF will challenge the notices in court unless they are withdrawn.

The Delhi Police has asked X to remove the Internet Freedom Foundation's account, six of its posts, the accounts of SFLC and @geoblockedindia, and posts by 16 other users, on the ground that they defame the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh. The posts document and comment on a legal notice sent in the RSS's name to IFF, SFLC and @geoblockedindia, which demanded that the three stop criticising and documenting government blocking orders. IFF received copies of the two police notices from X on the morning of 3 November 2026.
IFF calls on the Delhi Police to withdraw both notices. If they are not withdrawn, IFF will challenge them in court.

What has happened

On 29 October 2026 at 9:54 PM, IFF, SFLC and the operator of @geoblockedindia received a two-page "legal notice" said to be issued on behalf of the RSS. It asked the three to stop opposing the government's blocking directions, stop documenting restricted content, stop posting details of geo-blocked posts, and confirm in writing within seven days that they would comply. It was signed by an unnamed "Authorised Signatory". Several RSS office-bearers have since said on X that the notice is not authentic. IFF replied to the notice, wrote to the RSS at its official address asking whether it had authorised it, and published both the notice and its reply on 30 October.

On 31 October 2026 at 8:06 PM, the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime), Delhi Police, filed an "Illegal Content Report" with X (reference LD-321926). It listed two posts: IFF's post of 30 October on the notice, and SFLC post of the same day. The stated reason was that the posts are "defamatory towards the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh under Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023". The boxes for "safety/security", "defamation" and "other" were ticked. The fields for the nature of the court order and court order details were left empty. The desired action was "Remove/withhold content".

On 1 November 2026, a second notice arrived in the RSS's name. It said the matter had been handed to the Akhil Bharatiya Adhivakta Parishad, that complaints had been filed in several states, and that requests had been made to block IFF's X account and suspend the organisations. The Delhi Police had made its first request to X the previous evening. IFF did not know this until X told it on 3 November.

On 2 November 2026 at 8:51 AM, the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) filed a second notice with X (reference LD-322956). It lists 40 URLs. Thirty-seven are posts. Three are the entire accounts of @internetfreedom, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia. This time the boxes for "Hate speech", "defamation", "safety/security", "enforcement of court order" and "other" were all ticked. The court order fields were again left empty. The stated reason reads: "The posts constitute defamation and illegal content under Section 356 BNS. Under Rule 3(1)(d) of the IT Rules, 2021, read with Section 79(3)(b) IT Act, lawful notices require action within 3 hours."

The 16 other users are @ProdctiveUseful, @PanjwaniManoj, @jidge_, @RatanSharda55, @baxiabhishek, @SchrdingersDbag, @ashleshbiradar, @seemay, @NasirHussainINC, @Being_creat_ive, @AjoyDharmavaram, @othlaw, @_ananyaaa, @AimPoojaind, @incorigibleBhai and @rraoind. Their posts, as far as IFF can tell, comment on the notice or on the notice about it.

X forwarded both notice to IFF on 3 November 2026, at 8:47 AM and 10:03 AM, saying it was doing so "in the interest of transparency" and that IFF may wish to seek legal counsel and challenge the request in court. X's emails do not say that it has acted on the requests. The Delhi Police has not written to IFF, and no court has been approached, as far as the reports disclose. SFLC and @geoblockedindia have separately reported notifications from X about requests from the Uttar Pradesh Police, the Telangana Police and the Delhi Police's Cyber Crime unit, one of them against the whole of the @geoblockedindia account.

IFF's position

IFF condemns this legal action. A police force has made itself the enforcement arm of a private legal notice whose authenticity the organisation it names has not confirmed, and whose demand was that three organisations stop documenting censorship. The notices would deliver exactly what the notice asked for as they would also remove the accounts of the three groups in India that keep public records of what is blocked, and of who ordered it.

The posts in question are about a legal notice sent to us. They quote it, criticise how it was drafted, and say that we will carry on with our work. A person who receives a threat is entitled to publish it and answer it and that is not defamation of the sender. 

In the three weeks before the first notice, IFF assisted 86 people whose accounts were suspended or whose posts were withheld in India. SFLC's Free Speech Tracker recorded about 268 content restrictions and 83 account restrictions in the first 29 days of October. @geoblockedindia publishes the orders behind such blocks when platforms disclose them. None of this is unlawful. Documenting censorship and challenging it in court is what the Constitution expects of citizens.
IFF will not delete the posts. If the Delhi Police does not withdraw the notices, we will challenge them in court.

Why the reports are unlawful

Defamation is not a police matter. Section 356 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023 is a non-cognizable and bailable offence. Under Section 222 of the Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita, 2023, no court can take cognizance of it except on a complaint by the person aggrieved. 

Under Section 174 of the BNSS, the police cannot investigate a non-cognizable offence without an order of a Magistrate. The Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) is not the person aggrieved. The notices disclose no complaint by the RSS and no order of any Magistrate. Whether a statement is defamatory is for a court to decide after hearing its author, with the defences of truth, fair comment and good faith available to that author. 

In Subramanian Swamy v. Union of India, (2016) 7 SCC 221, the Supreme Court upheld criminal defamation on the strength of these safeguards. A police officer who asks a platform to remove speech as defamatory has decided the question himself, without a complainant, a court or a hearing.

The posts are protected comment. Exceptions 1 to 3 to Section 356(1) protect the truth published for the public good, opinion on the public conduct of public servants, and opinion on the conduct of any person touching a public question. The posts publish a notice that was sent to us and give our opinion of it. The RSS, if it sent the notice, chose to enter a public question. If it did not, the posts defame no one.

Further, Section 79(3)(b) and Rule 3(1)(d) do not permit this. In Shreya Singhal v. Union of India, (2015) 5 SCC 1, the Supreme Court read down Section 79(3)(b) so that an intermediary acquires "actual knowledge" only through a court order, or a notification from the appropriate government or its agency that unlawful acts relatable to Article 19(2) are being committed. The court said that it would be difficult for intermediaries to judge the legitimacy of the millions of requests they receive, and that the burden must not be placed on them. Rule 3(1)(d), as amended in November 2025 and February 2026, now requires the intimation to come from an officer not below the rank of Joint Secretary or Deputy Inspector General, to be reasoned, and to specify the legal basis and the nature of the unlawful act, subject to a monthly review by a Secretary-level officer. The three-hour window the notice invokes applies to a lawful order that meets these conditions. A web form that ticks "hate speech" and "enforcement of court order" while leaving the court order fields blank, and that gives one sentence of reasons for 40 URLs, is not such an order.

The notices by the Delhi Police are disproportionate. They seek to remove three accounts in their entirety, with years of posts, over six, four and eleven posts respectively. They sweep in 16 third parties whose only connection is that they commented on a public controversy. In Anuradha Bhasin v. Union of India, (2020) 3 SCC 637, the Supreme Court held that any restriction on speech must be necessary, proportionate and the least restrictive measure available, and that orders restricting speech must be published and reasoned. Removing an organisation's entire account for criticising a legal notice fails each of these tests.

The effect is to silence documentation of censorship and providing legal aid to Indian internet users. The accounts named are those that record blocking orders in India. The notice asked them to stop. A takedown request that accomplishes the demand of an anonymous private notice is not law enforcement. It is the use of state power for a private end, which Article 14 forbids.

Our demands

1. To the Delhi Police: Withdraw reports LD-321926 and LD-322956 and confirm the withdrawal in writing to X and to IFF. 

2. To the Delhi Police: Disclose the complaint on which the Special Commissioner of Police (Crime) acted, the authority under which the reports were filed, and whether any order of a Magistrate under Section 174 BNSS exists. Disclose every request made to any platform in this matter, including those made by the Cyber Crime unit against @geoblockedindia.

3. To X: Do not act on the reports. If any content is withheld in India, tell the affected user before acting, give them the full request, and name the legal basis. Publish both reports to the Lumen database, as the reporting form itself contemplates.

4. To the Ministry of Electronics and Information Technology and the Ministry of Home Affairs: Have the Secretary-level review required by Rule 3(1)(d) examine these intimations, and tell police forces that Rule 3(1)(d) is not a remedy for defamation, which the law reserves to the person aggrieved and to the courts.

5. To the RSS: State publicly whether it authorised either notice or any complaint to the police. If it did not, say so to the Delhi Police.

If the notices are not withdrawn, IFF will challenge them in court. We will continue to document blocking orders, to publish them, and to provide legal assistance to anyone whose account or post is withheld in India. Nothing in these notices changes that.

text:
Last night IFF, @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia received a legal notice said to be issued purportedly on behalf of the RSS. It’s hard to believe this comes from an organisation that has had a century to practise its paperwork and hence this may even be a weird prank! This notice asks us to stop criticising the Government’s blocking orders and stop documenting them. It also wants us to confirm in writing within seven days (seriously).

We can tell it’s an excellent teaching aid and here are seven lessons from it.

1) Say who you are: The notice names no advocate and gives no enrollment number. It is signed by an “Authorised Signatory” with no name. Replies go to a free Proton Mail ID, and the “office” is a residential flat in outer Delhi. A notice that can’t tell you who sent it is less a legal document than a weather event.

2) Have a grievance of your own: It never says how its client is harmed when we criticise a MeitY advisory. It complains on behalf of the Government’s blocking orders. The Union has no shortage of lawyers, and it hasn’t asked for volunteers.

3) Name the law: It threatens “appropriate legal action” under “the applicable provisions of law” and doesn’t cite a single section of any statute. A threat with no law, is literally an empty threat.

4) Don’t ask people to give up a fundamental right within seven days: The first demand is that we stop “publicly opposing” government directions. In Shreya Singhal (2015), the Supreme Court held that discussion and advocacy of a cause, however unpopular, sit at the heart of Article 19(1)(a). Opposing an order is how its legality gets tested. That is the Constitution working as intended.

5) Check whether the courts asked for the thing you want stopped” In Anuradha Bhasin (2020), the Supreme Court held that orders restricting fundamental rights must be made available so people can challenge them. The Reddit order is on the public Lumen Database because Reddit put it there. Reading a public database and saying what’s in it has a name. It’s called research.

6) Show us the spark and the powder keg: The notice says our work weakens national security measures, but it gives no instance, date or harm. In S. Rangarajan (1989), the Supreme Court held that the danger feared from speech can’t be remote, conjectural or far-fetched. It has to be like a spark in a powder keg. A post about a Lumen filing is not a spark.

7) Read it once more before you press send: The paragraphs run 1, then an empty 2 and 3, then 4. A PIN code wanders into the facts. The account it targets is on “Twitter”. 

Our reply is short. The notice is legally deficient because it makes no material allegation and cites no illegality. We will respectfully continue to advance constitutional rights, as we have done before. Notices like this rarely expect to win in court. They expect the recipient to get tired. We often are tired, but it has never changed what we do. Solidarity with @SFLCin and @geoblockedindia. 

If your post or account has been blocked in India, write to legal@internetfreedom.in.
